item.title: We Can Do for the Brain What Has Been Done for the Heart
item.description:
Neuroscience

We Can Do for the Brain What Has Been Done for the Heart

Improving our own brain health is within our grasp.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Mental health concerns cost the global economy trillions.
  • A three-year UT Dallas study showed that scalable brain health solutions exist.
  • Increased engagement in brain wellness programs led to measurable brain function changes.
  • Holistic brain health programs can help us advance brain wellness as we have our heart health.

It’s increasingly likely that you are a non-smoker who exercises, monitors your blood pressure, and eats thoughtfully to keep your cholesterol low.

You do these things because research has shown that they work better than almost any pharmaceutical. Your risk of dying of a heart attack at any age is now one-quarter of what it was in 1950.

But while heart health is thriving, the health of an equally important organ, the brain, is not doing so well. Rates of anxiety, depression, loneliness, substance abuse, cognitive problems, and dementia are rising across all ages.

“But,” I can hear you say, “the brain is different, right? We can have some control over heart health, but not brain health – that’s out of our hands and all determined by genetics, isn’t it?”

Brain Health Is Not Beyond Our Control

Not so, a major three-year study from UT Dallas published in the journal Scientific Reports has discovered.

Approximately 4,000 healthy people aged 19-94 volunteered to have their brain health assessed using an online index that gave a readout of three components of brain health: clarity of thinking and memory, emotional balance, and connectedness to people and purpose.

The index was presented not as a diagnosis or classifier but rather as a metric similar to a VO2 max measure of fitness that a physical trainer might give you to improve on. And improve, most participants did – not just over weeks, but for up to three years.

One of the participants—I’ll call him ‘John’—signed up for the Center for BrainHealth’s BrainHealth Project in his sixties when he was coping with a full-time job while caring for a family member with dementia. Like all participants, he was offered a call with a coach after his first assessment, then every three months thereafter.

The trained coach guided him toward a set of online training modules aimed at improving clarity of thinking and memory, building emotional balance and confidence, improving connectedness to people and purpose, and dealing with issues such as poor sleep. He also availed himself of daily ‘nudges’ sent to his cell phone by the program, reminding him to take steps toward implementing the skills he had learned in the online modules.

John's overall brain health index score increased by 33 percent over three years. He attributed these improvements to a number of changes he had made as a result of his engagement with the program. These included learning to use his brain differently by taking control of his attention, which allowed him to ‘switch gears without overheating.' He learned to ‘let the smaller things go,' take regular five-minute, technology-free ‘brain breaks,’ and build his social connectedness by becoming a more active listener. He used breathing techniques and other stress-management measures learned in the program, which helped him build resilience and keep emotional balance in the face of work and caregiving.

Another participant I'll call 'Kia,' a stay-at-home parent for the last 20 years, was in her fifties when she signed up for the study, mainly because she felt that her brain wasn’t working like it used to. She had a history of concussion, ADHD, and substance abuse and had dropped out of college without completing a degree. She initially focused on the sleep aspects of the program but gradually widened her engagement and used more of the brain health tools, modules, and nudges, all facilitated through her three monthly coaching sessions.

Her brain health index rose by 20 percent over two years. She said that she found the daily reminders of brain health nudges to be most helpful, and she also worked toward improving her connectedness by taking on a volunteer role.

The Link Between Brain Training and Improved Brain Health

This first-of-its-kind study offers strong scientific evidence to support the link between engaging in proactive brain training and improvements in brain health.

First, there was a dose-response relationship between how much people engaged with the program and how much their brain health index improved. Second, when participants moved to higher usage of the program’s support offerings, their index rose correspondingly. Finally, in a subset of the participants whose brains were imaged, improvements in the brain health index went hand in hand with visible improvements in brain function, with recent findings showing changes in the physical structure of the brain as well.

Ian Robertson
Source: Courtesy Ian Robertson

The mental health difficulties that arise from poor brain health are a modern-day scourge. Poor brain health affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, resulting in costs to the global economy of $5 trillion annually, a figure expected to rise to $16 trillion by 2030. Current therapies are simply not available or scalable to meet the needs of the vast numbers of people whose poor brain health causes immense problems to themselves, their families, and the country more broadly.

But this doesn’t need to be the case. This study demonstrates the potential of holistic programs aimed at improving brain health, including mental health, and points the way forward. It is clearly possible to drive improvement and recognize reasons to hope that we can take control of improving brain health in the same way that we have created progress for our heart health.

item.title: When an Adventure Changes You, Coming Home Can Be Hard
item.description:
Identity

When an Adventure Changes You, Coming Home Can Be Hard

Why returning home can feel strange when the person who returns has changed.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Wilderness adventures can shape how we understand ourselves and what matters most.
  • Returning home can feel difficult when you've changed, but your old life hasn't.
  • Time in nature can reveal more authentic ways of living.
  • Post-adventure discomfort can offer an invitation to integrate who you've become.
Shauni Bernau on the Pacific Crest Trail
Source: Shauni Bernau / Used with permission

Co-authored by Aimee Frazier and Shauni Bernau

Recently, I (Aimee) returned from a mountaineering expedition in the Olympic Mountains. Aside from a brief fall into a glacier crevasse, it was a fun and awe-inspiring trip.

It wasn’t the steep, technical snow or even my dreaded 45-pound pack that was the biggest challenge for me—it was the return home. When I returned to civilization and cell phone service, I felt totally overwhelmed. My phone had exploded with hundreds of text messages, enormous inbox alerts, and an immense pressure to jump right back into checking items off of the to-do list.

It was as if the experience had expanded me in some ways that made it difficult, and frankly a bit unappealing, to fit back into my regular life. It was a familiar feeling—one that I had experienced after other big adventures outdoors. As I processed it, I quickly realized I wasn’t the only one who'd felt this shock to the system after an outdoor adventure.

Stepping outside of our usual roles and routines can change how we see ourselves and bring clarity to what we value most in life. We often return with more than just stories to tell. We may also begin to question the parts of life that we step back into, as the person who returns from a trip no longer seems to fit comfortably into the life that they had previously built.

Shauni Bernau, a writer who thru-hiked the Pacific Crest Trail, experienced this on an even larger scale.

"I Wasn't Just Struggling to Return to My Old Life. I Was Questioning It"

In 2025, I (Shauni) hiked 2,000 miles on the Pacific Crest Trail. I lived in the wilderness for five months, and returning home was a shock to the system, to say the least. For 146 days, I was free of many of the obligations, expectations, and constant noise of ordinary life. The only thing I had to do was walk and think about where I would find and filter water and figure out where I would sleep.

And then I came home. I wasn't just struggling to return to my old life. I was questioning it. Almost overnight, life dragged me back into a thousand obligations, constant noise, daily decisions, and a sense of trying to keep up with endless demands. After months of near-silence, the noise back home seemed to have increased tenfold.

I felt myself falling back into the trap of everything needing to be faster and better. I became overwhelmed by the number of notifications on my phone and the daily "could we just circle back to this” emails at work. The trail had shown me another way of living, and the realization that my old life no longer aligned with my values.

On the trail, life was simpler, and I could just exist. Back home, I found myself going for walks and meditating partly to counterbalance the demands of everyday life. Thru-hiking had shown me the possibility of a different life—one that was slower and more mindful. Nothing about my life had dramatically changed while I was gone. But I had. I was returning to a culture I could suddenly see from the outside. And once you’ve experienced a drastically different way of living, it can be difficult to forget that it exists.

Before the trail, I tied much of my self-worth to productivity. I thought I was put on this earth to work as much as possible, to always be busy, and to surround myself with people who saw ambition as one of the highest virtues. But the trail challenged my idea of what a life well lived could look like. I found more meaning in spending time with loved ones, returning to childhood hobbies, and spending my days outside. I wanted to enjoy the little time we’re given on this earth. Because, as I finally realized, wanting to be happy is also an ambition.

Shauni Bernau at the end of the Pacific Crest Trail
Source: Shauni Bernau / Used with permission

When Adventure Changes the Self

Post-adventure depression is a common way of describing the emotional crash that can follow a major adventure. But something more complicated is taking place beneath the surface. Adventure experiences can change how we understand ourselves, as well as the lives we return to. Recent research regarding outdoor adventure suggests that experiences where we are immersed in nature can significantly influence people’s identities, influencing the way they understand themselves and who they wish to become (Froehly et al., 2025).

This process can be deeply existential. Our identities are shaped in part by our roles, relationships, environments, and the stories we tell about ourselves. A long, challenging wilderness experience can disrupt and re-organize an identity very quickly.

As Shauni experienced, extended time in the wilderness can strip away many of the structures that reinforce our identities. There are not many status markers outdoors. Your job title doesn’t help you find and filter water. Your salary can’t buy you a shortcut over a mountain pass. The way you dress and the size of your house suddenly become irrelevant.

Simultaneously, other parts of the self have room to emerge. We often discover that we are more capable than we thought, or learn that we can tolerate a large dose of physical challenge. We might even begin to step outside of constrictive cultural messages. And we may discover our sensory preferences—noticing that we feel better with less noise, more simplicity, more movement, or more time outside.

All of this new information that we gather about ourselves in the wilderness can lead to identity expansion. As both Shauni and I experienced, returning home can create an uncomfortable mismatch: We return changed, but the lives we left behind are the same. We are trying to fit a new understanding of ourselves into a life built around who we used to be.

The challenge of coming home, then, is not just about readjusting to daily life. It is also about navigating what to do with the person that you expanded into while you were away. Integrating what the experience taught you has value. And this is where post-adventure readjustment can become existential.

Instead of simply asking, How do I get used to being home again? We might ask: What actually matters to me now? Does the way I spend my time reflect what I now value? What parts of myself emerged out there that I want to hold onto? And how do I make room for that person here?

Of course, not every wilderness revelation means quitting your job or abandoning civilization. Nor should we romanticize the wilderness as the only place where an authentic or meaningful life is possible—that would not be sustainable or realistic. The goal of returning home may be much more subtle: to notice what the experience revealed about who you are and what you value now, and make room for those discoveries in everyday life. The goal is to let the person who came home have a say in what happens next.

Source: Shauni Bernau / Used with permission

About Shauni Bernau. After recovering from burnout, Shauni picked up an old childhood hobby and started hiking again. She found new meaning on the trail, and now tries to inspire other people to find meaning outside of the conventional paths in life.

item.title: The Proper Way to Report on Suicide
item.description:
Suicide

The Proper Way to Report on Suicide

Certain types of news coverage can lead to imitative behavior.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Too often, reporters cover suicide the same way they cover a crime.
  • Suicide should be covered as a public health issue with rates, treatment options, and resources.
  • Everyone should know and follow media guidelines of the American Association of Suicidology.

In this age of social media, few things remain secret for long. Moreover, humans have a predilection for gossip that often results in misleading and factually incorrect information being disseminated rapidly, widely, and indiscriminately. People have a responsibility to verify the accuracy of anything they tweet, post, or blog about before doing it. They also have a responsibility to consider the effect of their words on others.

In this regard, everyone would do well to follow the recommendations of the American Association of Suicidology to mainstream media when reporting on suicides:

  • Avoid sensationalistic headlines or subject lines.
  • Avoid using graphic photos or videos.
  • Avoid explicit descriptions of how someone died.
  • Avoid simplistic explanations for the death.

Instead of the headline, “Kurt Cobain Kills Himself with Shotgun,” for instance, news reports can say “Kurt Cobain Dead at Age 27.” Instead of photographing or filming where the death occurred, which only serves to draw people to the scene, the media can show the outside of a school or business where the person attended classes or worked, but not where he or she died. Instead of images of grieving family members, which can be a source of revenge for individuals who haven’t had good relations with parents or siblings, the media can use a yearbook, work, or family photo of the deceased. Instead of filming a well-attended memorial service, which can glorify the death in such a way as to cause others to imagine a similar outpouring of affection at their own death, the media can focus on close-ups of the printed program, a minister speaking, and floral arrangements while featuring a local crisis line number or the number 988. Choosing pictures with less emotional impact is contrary to the way the media operates, but is critical when covering suicide.

Also important is the way that the death is talked about. Instead of saying that someone’s suicide is inexplicable, impulsive, or happened without any previous indication of intent, media stories should include warning signs of suicide and information on what to do if someone you know exhibits these signs. Instead of reporting that someone’s suicide was preceded by a single event such as the recent loss of a job, the breakup of a marriage or relationship, or a failed test, reports should say that suicidal behavior is complex and usually is the result of multiple causes, including psychiatric illnesses that may not have been recognized or treated.

Too often, reporters cover a suicide the same way they cover a crime with a who, what, when, where, how, why mentality. Suicide isn’t a crime, however. It’s a public health issue and should be covered that way, with background information on trends, rates, treatment options, and resources. Equally important, a person’s suicide can be balanced with stories of hope and recovery in which suicidal thinking is overcome, and skills to cope with adversity are increased. This way, individuals and the media don’t unintentionally promote self-destructive behavior by contributing to suicide contagion but rather encourage people who are contemplating suicide to seek help.

At one time, the Annenberg Public Policy Center analyzed the coverage of suicides in nine major newspapers over a period of 12 months, plus three years’ worth of articles in the New York Times. Seven of the nine newspapers made a point of using the word suicide in at least half their headlines, sometimes in a sensational fashion. One headline in the New York Times was “Eighth-Grade Sweethearts in a Love Suicide.” In many of the Times’ articles, the Annenberg Center found, the method of suicide was mentioned in the headline, yet only 8 percent of the articles cited depression as a possible factor in the person’s death. Some of the journalists who were contacted by the center didn’t know that certain types of news coverage can lead to imitative behavior, and none were aware that experts in the field had developed media guidelines for reporting on suicide.[1] That is changing—slowly—although it’s still common for media reports to use the phrase “committed suicide.” Since the general public often takes its cue from the media, this stigmatizing terminology needs to end.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why Do People With ADHD Get Stuck in Overthinking?
item.description:
ADHD

Why Do People With ADHD Get Stuck in Overthinking?

Five ways to quiet your inner critic and break the cycle.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Overthinking isn't a sign of weakness or indecisiveness but reflects executive functioning challenges.
  • Intense emotions and past experiences shape patterns of self-criticism that lead to rumination.
  • Rumination involves worries with no solution while reflection leads to personal growth and change.
  • Practicing a good enough mindset builds confidence in ways that perfectionism does not.
Source: ninitta/iStock photo ID:1889949598

You finally hit "send" on the email. Five minutes later, you're replaying it in your mind. “Did that sound rude? Should I have explained more? What if they took it the wrong way?” By bedtime, you've gone over the exchange a dozen times.

Many adults with ADHD describe feeling like their minds are always "on." One thought leads to another until what started as a simple concern becomes an exhausting spiral of worry, self-doubt, and second-guessing. Overthinking often reflects the ways that executive functioning challenges, emotional dysregulation, anxiety, and years of negative feedback can intersect for adults with ADHD. Unfortunately, careful review can easily turn into rumination. Understanding why you overthink can help you change your relationship with it. Instead of getting pulled into every thought, you can learn to notice what's happening, step out of the loop, and respond differently.

Why ADHD Makes Overthinking So Common

Overthinking isn't simply "thinking too much." Often, your brain attempts to reduce uncertainty, prevent mistakes, or protect you from disappointment, embarrassment, or rejection. The harder you try to think your way out of uncomfortable feelings, the more stuck you can become. Here are some reasons that ADHD makes overthinking so common.

Your Working Memory Is Carrying Too Much

Working memory is like your brain's mental sticky note. It helps you hold information in mind while you complete a task, solve a problem, or make a decision. For adults with ADHD, working memory can require extra effort. You may find yourself mentally juggling unfinished tasks, conversations, worries, appointments, and reminders all at once. When your working memory is overloaded, it's harder to determine what deserves your attention and what you can safely let go.

Big Emotions Can Make Thoughts Feel Bigger

Difficulties with emotional regulation are common for many adults with ADHD and can intensify thoughts that accompany disappointment, frustration, embarrassment, or uncertainty. A small mistake can suddenly feel enormous. For instance, a delayed text can become evidence that someone is upset. As emotional intensity rises, so does the urgency to figure out what happened and fix it. But urgency doesn't always mean something requires immediate attention. Sometimes it means your nervous system is activated. Trying to think harder rarely settles things. Regulating yourself first usually works better.

Past Experiences Shape Your Inner Critic

Many adults with ADHD have spent years hearing: "You need to try harder." "You're so smart—you just don't apply yourself." "Why do you always forget?" Eventually, these external voices can become internal ones. Your inner critic may believe that if it reviews everything you do and anticipates every possible mistake, it can protect you from criticism or rejection. In this way, your inner critic isn't simply trying to make you feel bad. It's attempting—ineffectively—to keep you safe. Unfortunately, its tools are self-doubt, criticism, and impossible standards. Instead of increasing confidence, they reinforce anxiety and shame.

Anxiety and ADHD Influence Each Other

ADHD and anxiety frequently co-occur. ADHD-related challenges with uncertainty, inconsistent attention, working memory, and anticipating consequences can collide with anxiety's desire for certainty. So you analyze—and then analyze your analysis. You review a conversation, consider possible interpretations, and prepare responses to things that haven't happened. But certainty rarely arrives. Overthinking can feel productive because your mind is busy working on the problem. Yet analysis isn't the same as action. At some point, thinking stops helping you move forward and starts keeping you stuck.

Five Ways to Quiet Your Inner Critic

The goal isn't to stop thinking. It's to recognize when thinking has stopped being useful and choose what to do next.

1. Learn the Difference Between Reflection and Rumination

Reflection asks: "What can I learn from this?" Rumination asks: "Why did I do that? What if I messed everything up?" Reflection helps you gain information and move forward. Rumination circles around the same worries. When you notice yourself looping, ask: "Am I solving a problem, or am I replaying one?" If there's a concrete action you can take, identify it. If there isn't, your task becomes letting the thought pass rather than trying to solve it.

2. Challenge Your Inner Critic Instead of Automatically Believing It

Thoughts aren't facts, even when they feel convincing. When your inner critic says, "Everyone thinks I sounded stupid," slow down and ask: “What's the evidence? What's another possible explanation? What would I say to a friend?” You don't need to replace every negative thought with a positive one. Aim for something balanced and accurate. Try: "I stumbled over what I wanted to say, but that doesn't mean the whole conversation went badly." That's not letting yourself off the hook. It's putting the situation into perspective.

3. Get Your Thoughts Out of Your Head

The ADHD brain doesn't benefit from holding dozens of reminders, worries, ideas, and unfinished tasks in working memory. Externalize them. Use the Notes app, keep a notebook nearby, make a checklist, or record a voice memo. If you're worried about forgetting something, put it somewhere you trust instead of rehearsing it repeatedly. Then ask: Does this need my attention now, later, or not at all? Externalizing information reduces the pressure to keep everything in your head and makes it easier to identify priorities and act.

4. Practice "Good Enough"

Many adults with ADHD develop perfectionistic habits after years of trying to avoid mistakes, criticism, or disappointing others. Unfortunately, perfectionism can lead to procrastination, avoidance, decision paralysis, and more self-doubt. Instead of asking, "Is this perfect?" Try: "Is this good enough to move forward?" Perhaps the email doesn't need another revision. "Good enough" doesn't mean careless. It means recognizing the difference between doing something well and endlessly trying to eliminate every possible imperfection. Progress builds confidence in ways that perfectionism rarely does.

5. Strengthen Your Inner Coach

You may not be able to silence your inner critic completely, but you can strengthen another voice alongside it. I think of this as your inner coach: the part of you that acknowledges what's difficult without attacking you for struggling.

  • Instead of "Why can't I get anything right?" try: "This is hard right now. What's one small step I can take?"
  • Instead of "I always mess things up," try: "I don't like how that went. What would I like to do differently next time?"

Self-compassion isn't lowering your standards or ignoring accountability. It's responding to yourself with enough kindness and perspective to learn from what happened. For adults with ADHD who have spent years judging themselves harshly, developing this different internal voice takes practice.

A Final Thought

Source: fizkes/iStock photo ID:2232987560

If you've spent years replaying conversations, questioning your decisions, or worrying that you've gotten things wrong, consider what your overthinking is trying to accomplish. Perhaps it's trying to prevent another mistake, protect you from criticism or rejection, or find certainty where certainty isn't available.

Instead, notice the loop. Settle yourself. Look for the facts. Decide whether you can take action, and take one small step. The goal isn't to stop thinking. It's to recognize when your thoughts have shifted from helping you solve a problem to keeping you stuck in one. With practice, your inner critic doesn't have to be the loudest voice in the room. You can strengthen your inner coach instead and move forward with greater confidence, clarity, and peace.

item.title: When a Good Parent Has Something to Regret
item.description:
Parenting

When a Good Parent Has Something to Regret

What we can learn from the unintended consequences of love.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Good intentions on the part of parents do not prevent painful consequences for their children.
  • Taking responsibility for how we have parented is not the same as accepting blame or condemning ourselves.
  • Regret about the past becomes valuable when it changes how we relate to our young adult child in the present.
Source: William Cho/Pixabay

A considerable challenge in the work that I do with my patients is helping them to distinguish between responsibility and culpability, which is often a difficult distinction to make. Something done deliberately is different from something done accidentally, and an accident resulting from negligence differs from an accident that was truly unavoidable.

But just because we are not culpable does not mean that we have nothing to think about, nothing to ponder—and nothing to regret. This is particularly relevant when it comes to parents of young adult children.

Let’s examine the relationship between 50-year-old Donovan and his 23-year-old daughter, Inez. Their relationship has grown uncomfortably distant over the last several years, and they finally agree, at Donovan’s urging, to make some time to sit down with me and sort things out.

Inez tearfully admits, “You were a tyrant, Dad, you pushed me and pushed me in school and I never felt like I was doing enough, never felt like I was good enough. You wouldn’t let me go out with friends, you wouldn’t let me play any sports, everything was school, school, school. I grew up feeling like I was a terrible disappointment to you, that I was worth nothing.”

Donovan, of course, feels terrible as he learns more about the ways in which he made his daughter so miserable growing up. But, as he thinks about it in a subsequent individual session with me, he considers the possibility that one of the reasons he drove Inez so hard was because he grew up with a younger sister, Estella, who never finished high school, who became addicted to opiates, who gave birth to a child at the age of 17 and put that child up for adoption, and who is currently living a marginal existence at the age of 47.

So, Donovan has begun to conceive of an explanation for why he fathered Inez in the way that he did. He obviously didn’t want to torment her, he just wanted to protect her from re-creating his younger sister’s dismal life. But, nevertheless, from Inez’s standpoint, he was an overly demanding, ruthless, and unyielding dad.

Donovan clearly feels regret, but where can it take him when it comes to healing his relationship with his daughter? Here are some possible pathways:

  1. He can stick with his burgeoning (and very legitimate) explanation of his behavior as a way of justifying it, letting himself completely off the hook (exoneration and vindication).
  2. He can accuse Inez of not appreciating how hard he was working to protect her from following his sister’s dark pathways (blaming).
  3. He can make a quid-pro-quo agreement with Inez—“I’ll admit I was too hard on you if you admit that I was a good father and doing my very best” (conditional).
  4. He can become consumed by self-loathing and commit to punishing himself for having failed as a father (ashamed).
  5. He can live in the in-between: “I really did mean well, and I now am beginning to comprehend why I behaved the way I did, but nevertheless, my daughter was deeply hurt by my behavior. I want to take responsibility for my part in that and allow what I am hearing and learning from her to change the kind of father I have been into the kind of father she now deserves to have.”

Just because we are not completely culpable for causing someone else pain does not mean that we turn away from the reality that they are in pain and that we may have played a role—inadvertent as it may have been—in bringing about their pain.

Experiencing regret is not the same as declaring that our behavior was morally unprincipled, malicious, or negligent. Nor does it have to result in vigorously disputing the validity of another person’s experience.

But to make our regret meaningful, we have to mourn the difference between the kind of parent that we intended to be, and the kind of parent we actually were in our children’s eyes. The reality is that, as loving, imperfect people, we valiantly strive to make good decisions in our important relationships that may nevertheless result in unplanned, unforeseen outcomes.

So what we want to consider is that an acknowledgment of regret does not have to automatically be conflated with a confession that we are at fault or to blame. In the case of Donovan and Inez, it is not necessary for him to conclude that he was a vile or despicable parent in order to feel constructive regret about the ways in which being his daughter was frequently trying and arduous for her.

We can grieve an outcome without having to torture or exile ourselves, or put ourselves on permanent, Kafkaesque trial. None of these approaches have anything to do with healing, nor will they help us to make amends and attempt to repair a relationship that may have been injured or damaged. In fact, they actually impede the very repair that may be longed for.

item.title: “You Look Tired”
item.description:
Beauty

“You Look Tired”

What to do when someone else’s comment makes you suddenly self-conscious.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • "You look tired" can trigger sudden self-consciousness and shift your self-perception instantly.
  • Even well-intended appearance comments can increase body dissatisfaction and self-doubt.
  • Compliments on appearance—even positive—often cause discomfort, especially in professional settings.
  • Not every perception from others deserves authority over how you see yourself.
Source: peoplecreations / Freepik

“You look tired.”

It’s hard to know what to say in response. Saying “Thanks” might sound sarcastic. Saying “I’m fine” can sound a little defensive. If you ask, “Do I really look that bad?” you’ve invited someone to provide a more detailed commentary on your appearance, which you probably didn’t want in the first place.

Usually the person means no harm. They may even be trying to show concern. Still, the comment can change your experience of yourself almost instantly. A moment earlier, you were thinking about the meeting, the conversation, or whatever you were doing. Now you’re wondering what your face looks like. Do I look older today? Are my eyes puffy? Do I look sick? Is everyone else noticing this too?

Now you’re seeing yourself through their eyes, whether you wanted to or not.

That shift is one of the questions I explore in my forthcoming book, Being Seen. Other people’s perceptions inevitably become part of how we understand ourselves, but sometimes they arrive when we didn’t ask for them. A casual remark may stay with us long after the person who made it has moved on.

When a Comment Changes What You Notice

We can learn a great deal about ourselves through other people. They can tell us that we seem confident, distracted, intimidating, funny, anxious, warm, or distant. Sometimes they notice things we genuinely can’t see from the inside. That information can be very useful, but it can also make us acutely self-conscious.

Research on appearance comments shows how quickly this can happen in everyday life. Liu and colleagues (2022) asked 620 adults to use a phone app six times a day for a week, reporting whether they had recently received comments about their appearance and how dissatisfied they felt with their bodies at that moment. Negative appearance comments predicted greater body dissatisfaction, while positive appearance comments predicted lower body dissatisfaction. The study didn’t examine “you look tired” specifically, but it shows how a passing comment from someone else can change how people feel about their appearance in the course of an ordinary day.

“You look tired” is more ambiguous than an explicitly critical comment about weight or attractiveness because it can be presented as concern for your well-being. Yet it still directs your attention toward an aspect of your appearance you may not have been thinking about at all. You weren’t studying your eyes or wondering how worn out you looked five seconds earlier. Now you might be.

Why Are People So Comfortable Saying It?

We notice plenty of things about other people that we keep to ourselves. You might notice that a colleague looks older than the last time you saw her, that someone’s skin has changed, or that a friend has gained weight. Most of us have learned that noticing something doesn’t mean we need to announce it, especially if the observation might make the person uncomfortable.

Tiredness seems to be treated differently. Maybe that’s because fatigue sounds temporary, allowing “you look tired” to be framed as concern rather than criticism. With someone you know well, noticing that they look different may also feel like evidence that you’re paying attention and are interested in their well-being. The intention can be caring while the effect is still awkward.

Appearance comments can be unsettling even when they’re positive. In two experiments using simulated job interviews, women who received compliments about their appearance reported more anxiety and depressive affect than women who were complimented on their competence (Pacilli et al., 2023). The studies weren’t about fatigue, and being told you look beautiful is obviously different from being told you look tired. But they demonstrate that favorable attention to appearance can still be uncomfortable when appearance is irrelevant to the situation and the person expects to be evaluated for something else.

That is part of what can make “you look tired” especially unwelcome at work. You may want your ideas, judgment, or competence to be the focus. Instead, someone has made your face part of the conversation.

Resist the Urge to Investigate

The comment often gains power from what happens after it’s been made. You may feel the urge to check your reflection, wonder exactly what the person noticed, or look for confirmation from someone else. A passing remark can turn into a rigorous investigation of your own face.

There is a useful distinction between hearing the comment and treating it as evidence that requires further exploration. The person may have picked up on something real, or they may have responded to lighting, expression, age, makeup, a long day, or simply the way you looked at that particular moment. Their perception doesn’t need to be dismissed, but it doesn’t deserve automatic authority and validation either.

This is one of the complications of being seen. Other people sometimes notice things about us that we can’t see ourselves, and sometimes that information is useful. The problem starts when one person’s observation expands into an imagined consensus. Instead of simply knowing that someone thought you looked tired, you begin wondering whether everyone sees you that way.

Other people will always form impressions of us, and sometimes they’ll tell us what they see. The challenge is deciding which impressions are worth taking in. “You look tired” may tell you how you appeared to one person in one moment. It doesn’t have to tell you anything more.

item.title: A Middle Way Can Shift Systems and Attitudes
item.description:
Empathy

A Middle Way Can Shift Systems and Attitudes

Personal Perspective: We need a vibrant center for all people.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • A vibrant center is not a complacent middle, but an active, conscious encounter with the paradoxes of life.
  • The vibrant center is based on three pillars: presence, openness to experience, and discernment.
  • We need to elect leaders who embody a vibrant-centered consciousness to survive let alone thrive.

As a psychologist with over 40 years of clinical experience, it is clear to me that our suffering as a nation is more than just political or cultural; it is profoundly psychospiritual. It is at the heart of our freedom to live—and let live. Can we hold contrasting, even contradictory, views without destroying each other? In this light, I’ve long recognized that most—if not all—power centers throughout history based their leadership on a pre-set dogma, royal bloodlines, or reactive tyranny.

The U.S., however, has been a real bewilderment for me (and I know for many of us). How could a country that was founded on a deliberative, evolving idea—that all people are created equal, with a right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness—be the same country that committed a virtual genocide on the native peoples of its land; that enslaved people; and that treated women and other marginalized groups as second-class citizens?

And then it struck me: We’re in over our heads! This is why the American Experiment has been so rare throughout history. People have known how difficult it is for a democratic republic to flourish. This conundrum struck me especially hard recently when my wife and I saw the current Tony Award-winning play Schmigadoon! On the surface, it is a play about a couple from New York City who began their relationship with the liveliness and glee many couples in contemporary America start with. But the play goes much deeper.

After the opening scenes, we find the couple years later hiking aimlessly in the woods and bickering about trivialities. They seem to be hollow and lacking in values. Then they come upon a fantasy town called Schmigadoon—which is not really a fantasy. It was a metaphor. A powerful metaphor for the supreme irony I was talking about. This town became the setting for all the ills, yet also marvels of the American story.

The town appeared happy; the people were free, working joyfully and having fun. That is, until the New Yorkers arrived, the “outsiders.” And the town's truer colors bled through, like a Pleasantville.

The New Yorkers bring a curiosity and deeper autonomy that the town elders can’t tolerate. Like so many homogeneous cultures, the townspeople turn against these interlopers. They turn against their questioning of religion, routine, and town hierarchy. In sum, the New Yorkers are radically “othered.” They are a grave threat to the order, purity, and serenity that, at least on the surface, permeate Schmigadoon’s culture.

But soon the cracks in this surface begin to show, as the mayor acknowledges being gay, and the little African American boy, who was disparaged for being “different,” begins to feel more empowered, largely due to the man from New York who affirms him. By the end of the play, the staid, buttoned-up doctor shows real emotion as he falls in love with the woman from New York who helps him open up, and even the extremely shy husband of the town matriarch, who epitomizes puritanical values, acknowledges that he’s gay.

The man from New York begins to fall for the teacher who carries out her duties with love and affection for her students, and the traditional values of community, loyalty, and security begin to impress both New Yorkers, and their own relationship improves. In the end, they realize that both tradition and faith are vital to deepening their relationship, and to life itself. The townfolk also recognize the virtues of greater freedom, spontaneity, and curiosity. The upshot is that what was fear-driven and filled with stereotypes, such as the chaos exemplified by the town’s fear of the New Yorkers’ liberalism, or the oppression imagined by the New Yorkers’ fear of the town’s conservatism, has now morphed into a mutual recognition of the nuggets of validity in both.

Upon further reflection, I see that the founders’ vision of America was just that, a vision. It’s a vision that is virtually unprecedented in human history, and still not ready for prime time. What is clear is that, like the players in Schmigadoon, many if not most of us live fear-based rather than presence-based lives. The townspeople in Schmigadoon, like many staunch conservatives, are terrified of the changes the New Yorkers bring to their predictable—yet too often wooden—lives. And the New Yorkers, like many ardent liberals, are aghast at small-town culture and its rigidities. Yet also blind to the bonds and time-honored wisdom they contain.

Still, the play offers a clue at its end, not only about how these particular players could mend their stodgy ways, but how society could follow suit. This clue is about what it takes to become livelier and more enriched: people who talk to each other, participate in each other’s rituals, and get to know each other as people rather than media-created clichés.

The shift from fear-based to aware- or experience-based can be called a “vibrant center.” The vibrant center holds contrasting, and even contradictory, positions at the same time. That tension enables a more present, open, and discerning way of life. The vibrant center is not moderation or a complacent middle. It is an active, conscious stance that attunes more to circumstance than presumption, more to what deeply matters than expedience. The vibrant center is linked to human resilience, or what psychologist George Bonnano calls a “flexibility mindset.” This mindset sees “otherness” as a chance for growth, not a threat to be managed.

If we want to truly move toward a democratic republic in our society and world, we need to stop throwing the proverbial baby out with the bathwater and be open to the nuggets of wisdom in both liberalism and conservatism. We need to find that pivot point of choice and discernment rather than being driven by fears and stereotypes, dread, and dogma, which provide escape, but also narrowness, narcissism, and destruction.

We can stop being driven by our lizard brains and capitulation to power brokers, and start grappling with the kind of lives we really want to live. We can embrace grassroots movements that foster supportive, structured dialogue between groups of contrasting cultural and political backgrounds. We can thrive and not just survive. To do otherwise is to face annihilation, either by our fellow humans or by the grotesque instruments that we produce.

item.title: Connection Is the Heart of Thriving Teams and Culture
item.description:
Leadership

Connection Is the Heart of Thriving Teams and Culture

Why connection is the superpower for improving team cohesion and culture.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • The 5Cs evidence-based model for improving teams and culture shows connection is the most important element.
  • Recent research shows trust and care are foundational for teams to reach their full potential.
  • Leaders can start fostering connection by acknowledging and showing care for the whole person.

There is a concerning downward trend in the workforce that’s hindering team and culture performance.

Employees’ trust in leadership and their belief that the organization cares about their well-being have remained near record lows in 2026, according to Gallup.

While the concepts of trust and well-being aren’t typically linked in organizations, they are, in fact, interconnected.

In developing the 5Cs model, a scientifically validated model that captures the five critical elements that create high-performing teams and thriving cultures, we discovered that the element of connection is crucial: It reflects the level of connection everyone feels with each other, and it encompasses the sub-factors of trust and well-being.

The 5Cs research results highlight that trust and well-being are foundational for teams and organizations to reach their full potential. Working in environments where we trust and care holistically for each other boosts all other areas.

Unfortunately, organizations often struggle with not having a roadmap or knowing where to focus to move the needle on these areas, as demonstrated by the declines in both trust and well-being.

My recent book, Connected Culture, provides a roadmap for leaders to build high-performing teams and thriving cultures with the 5Cs model. The five elements are: Connection, Candid Communication, Clarity, Collaboration, and Contribution. In a series of five posts, I’ll dive into each element in depth, starting with connection.

Overview of the Connection Element of the 5Cs

What it means: Connection within a team and organization reflects the ties that everyone feels with the entity’s ethos and with their colleagues. Connection encapsulates a deep sense of mutual trust that goes beyond mere association or involvement, and well-being that includes the physical, mental, and emotional health of members of the team and organization.

The Subfactors:

  • Well-being is a measure of the emphasis placed on physical, mental, and emotional health by the team or organization.
  • Trust refers to the trustworthiness and mutual trust that is fostered and reflected within the team or organization.

Recent research results reveal that connection is the superpower for improving team cohesion and culture. The key reasons are:

  • Connection is the most important ring of the 5Cs.
  • The Connection ring impacts every other ring more significantly than the others.
  • Connection is the individual element most predictive of job satisfaction, though all 5Cs combined are more predictive.

Challenges When Connection Is Low:

Low connection environments don’t allow teams and organizations to produce the maximum level of results. People often feel isolated or disconnected from their peers or the organization’s culture. Overall, it creates an environment where all other elements of the 5Cs suffer—it’s not possible to reach high levels of the other elements.

Low levels of trust have physiological implications and actually change our brain chemistry. Low trust is linked with being in a state of increased fear, where we feel threatened, act reactively, don’t have access to think clearly, and create silos. It’s not an environment where people can do their best work or lean on each other.

When well-being is low, individuals don’t feel like the organization adequately supports their well-being. People don’t feel like they are cared about as whole people, that self-care is valued, or that their mental health is supported. Low levels of well-being can impact an employee's overall satisfaction and performance. It creates a negative environment, adversely impacting individuals, teams, and the organization.

Benefits When Connection Is High

Environments of high trust and care create an upward spiral of openness and engagement. To the outside, it can look like teams are accomplishing the impossible. Magic happens when what teams and organizations can accomplish is much greater than the sum of their parts.

High connection is the heart of how organizations accomplish all aspects of what they want to achieve.

High-performing teams work effectively together, lean on each other and get into positive cycles for their own growth.

In a high-trust environment, people feel safe, collaborate, and have access to their full cognitive abilities. In "The Neuroscience of Trust" HBR article, Paul Zak discovered through his research: “People at high-trust companies report: 74% less stress, 106% more energy at work, 50% higher productivity, 13% fewer sick days, 76% more engagement, 29% more satisfaction with their lives, 40% less burnout.”

When well-being is high, everyone demonstrates they care about people mentally, physically, and emotionally, which allows teams and organizations to progress to the next level of performance. Gallup found that when employees believe their organization cares about their overall well-being, they are over 4 times more engaged, 7 times more likely to recommend their organization, 73% less likely to feel burned out at work, 53% less likely to be looking for a job, and 50% more likely to thrive in life.

Leaders Can Foster Connection by Showing They Care

To acknowledge and show care for the whole person, create a dialogue around well-being and be open to speaking about it. I encourage leaders to share their own journeys with well-being. When they do so, they model caring for their well-being and give permission for the team to do the same. It doesn’t mean you need to expose your personal life. It does mean we can care about each other more holistically, and not just for our productivity.

Leaders, you can open a conversation with your team by asking: How are we caring for ourselves and each other as a team, as humans?

Ultimately, the connection element of the 5Cs emphasizes bringing greater humanity into the workplace. We must place trust and well-being at the center of how organizations operate and integrate both aspects into how we approach improving leaders, teams, and organizations.

item.title: Thriving With Adult Pathological Demand Avoidance
item.description:
Autism

Thriving With Adult Pathological Demand Avoidance

Understanding your demand avoidance and building a life that works for you

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • PDA is an autism profile marked by a strong need for autonomy and intense resistance to everyday demands.
  • Avoidance, mood shifts, and anxiety can strain work, relationships, and routine tasks for adults with PDA.
  • Self-understanding, accommodations, and flexible work settings help adults with PDA preserve energy.
  • Allies, online communities, self-advocacy, and a knowledgeable coach can help them build a meaningful life.

Living with pathological demand avoidance (PDA) as an autistic adult often involves intense resistance to everyday expectations. A constant internal need for autonomy shapes work and relationships, and that can make life feel overwhelming.

Adults with PDA frequently describe difficulty feeling understood, maintaining connections, and managing daily responsibilities. With the right strategies and support, a fulfilling life that honors neurodivergence is possible.

Source: Keira Burton / Pexels

Understanding PDA in Adulthood

PDA is described as a profile within the autism spectrum, marked by an overwhelming need to maintain control over one’s life and to resist demands. It is not a formal diagnosis in the DSM-5-TR or ICD-11, and researchers continue to debate how it relates to autism more broadly, but a significant number of adults resonate deeply with its descriptions.

Its most recognizable trait is that when someone asks whether you want to do something, the automatic response is often “no,” even for activities you genuinely want to pursue.

Common experiences include:

  • Extreme avoidance of requests or expectations, including seemingly reasonable ones
  • Sudden mood shifts when demands arise
  • Procrastination on tasks that feel like obligations
  • Reflexive deflection through language or white lies driven by anxiety

These patterns affect employment, relationships, and everyday tasks. Following instructions, meeting deadlines, and navigating workplace dynamics can become difficult. Communication barriers and fear of losing autonomy strain romantic and platonic relationships alike. Even routine errands or appointments can feel insurmountable.

The Power of Understanding Yourself

PDA has long been viewed through a deficit lens, and a growing number of voices describe it as a different way of being. Measuring oneself against neurotypical standards tends to deepen shame, but recognizing that a brain works differently can open the door to strategies that increase your quality of life.

Understanding how PDA traits influence thoughts, feelings, and behaviors lays the foundation for effective management. With self-acceptance, you can then shift your attention to appreciating your genuine strengths and develop personalized coping strategies.

Source: RDNE Stock project / Pexels

Your Unique Strengths

While PDA presents challenges, it also brings valuable traits. A strong sense of autonomy and determination often shows up as unwavering dedication to personal passions. Intense focus and attention to detail in areas of interest can become real advantages in professions and hobbies where deep expertise develops.

Building Supportive Connections

Embracing your authentic self becomes easier when you are surrounded by people who understand your neurodivergence. Seek online communities where you can connect with other adults with PDA. Sharing experiences and strategies provides validation and empowerment.

For those closest to you, educational resources like the Thrive Autism Coaching blog can help them understand you better and create a supportive environment where you truly thrive. A coach who understands PDA can also provide tailored support.

Practical Strategies for Daily Life

Creating Low-Demand Environments

Minimizing demands is one of the most commonly recommended management approaches. At home, daily blocks of time with zero expectations allow recovery. Family members and housemates who help create sanctuary periods make it easier to balance everyone’s needs.

In workplace and social settings, accommodations such as flexible schedules, privacy, and quiet spaces can help reduce sensory demands and preserve energy.

Source: Tima Miroshnichenko / Pexels

Finding Fulfilling Work

Careers aligned with personal interests and strengths are ideal, but rigid traditional structures are often challenging for adults with PDA. Settings that offer greater autonomy, such as startups, freelancing, remote work, and entrepreneurship, tend to be a better match and allow people to thrive on their own terms.

Caring for Body and Mind

Stress and burnout can intensify PDA traits, increasing avoidance and emotional dysregulation. Adequate sleep, exercise, nutrition, and hydration form the foundation, because gaps in any of these areas make PDA harder to manage. With the basics covered, practices that calm the nervous system, such as meditation, calming hobbies, time in nature, or time with pets, add further support.

When these strategies are not enough, awareness of personal triggers helps. Recognizing your triggers early makes it possible to apply coping strategies before reaching a breaking point.

Advocating for Yourself

Advocacy creates more inclusive environments. Some people are unwilling to learn about neurodivergence, and some are open to it. When someone is willing, sharing resources and personal experiences builds understanding. Specific examples showing how adjustments benefit everyone involved clarify needs, and a network of allies and supporters makes a significant difference in daily life.

Moving Forward

Living with PDA as an adult can feel isolating, yet many individuals now share their experiences publicly. Positive role models and stories validate lived experience and highlight what is possible.

Source: Alena Darmel / Pexels

A supportive community that appreciates unique perspectives matters, and an autism life coach can be a transformative partner in discovering who you are.

Navigating adulthood with PDA takes courage, and confidence and joy are within reach through personal growth and empowerment. Understanding needs, embracing authenticity, and putting practical strategies in place can pave the way for a meaningful life.

Small victories deserve celebration. Every successful communication of a need, every recharge in a low-demand space, and every overcome obstacle demonstrates resilience. These accomplishments, however small they seem, are significant steps toward living life on one’s own terms.

item.title: The Psychology of Narcissism Versus Healthy Self-Esteem
item.description:
Narcissism

The Psychology of Narcissism Versus Healthy Self-Esteem

Too much praise can nurture imposters and narcissists.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy self-esteem and narcissism have distinct features and consequences and do not lie on a continuum.
  • People are inherently biased towards overestimating their own performance, intelligence, and skills.
  • Narcissism is cultivated in children by overpraising them, focusing on social status and being outstanding.
  • Overconfidence, certainty, and the absence of doubt are the enemies of critical thinking.
Source: bulatsilva / iStock

Are we encouraging healthy self-esteem, or breeding a culture of narcissism, overconfidence, and inauthenticity when we “like,” act impressed by, or otherwise contribute to people’s inflated perceptions of their skills, knowledge, and attributes?

Overconfidence and certainty, by definition, are the enemies of critical thinking, which is the basis of intelligent judgment, problem-solving, and decision-making. Critical thinking involves curiosity, healthy doubt, and the deliberate consideration of how one’s conclusion might be wrong.

Inherent Bias Towards Overestimating One’s Own Abilities

Even without encouragement, people are inherently biased towards inaccurate, overly positive appraisals of themselves, believing they are better than their peers in terms of personality, qualities, and abilities (Zell et al., 2020). Predictably, less skillful people who perform poorly are even more likely to confidently miscalibrate their performance, overestimating how well they will do and, afterward, how well they did (Coutinho et al., 2024; Karaca et al., 2023).

Grandiose narcissists already believe they are superior to others and maintain their idealized self-image through seeking status, admiration, and dominance and doing so effectively (Kaufman et al., 2020). Blunted neural sensitivity in the error detection part of their brains further facilitates the ability to ignore contradictory evidence. (Robins et al., 2025).

Rise in Swagger Culture

A recent column in the New York Times (Sobrevilla, 2026) identified a cultural rise in swagger and a decrease in buzz about imposter syndrome.

In a social climate that rewards inflated confidence over accountability, accuracy, and appropriate humility, now, instead of imposter syndrome being in vogue, it’s normative and even popular to be an actual imposter (knowingly or not).

With imposter syndrome, people ignore evidence of their achievements and fear being exposed as a “fraud.” This phenomenon (not a medical syndrome) is associated with anxiety, perfectionism, self-doubt, and underestimating one’s competencies (Bravata et al., 2020). Not surprisingly, imposter syndrome is more prevalent among highly accomplished women adapting to the norms of environments such as academia (Feenstra et al., 2020).

Imposter syndrome proliferates in social discourse in certain contexts because it’s an easy, even desirable, condition to claim publicly since it implicitly authenticates one’s achievements and competencies, while packaging them in the humility and derogation that can feel safer, particularly to women, in competitive male-dominated environments.

In contrast, the trend we see in communal digital spaces, politically and beyond, is for people with no achievements to pose as experts, boasting with unearned confidence in the guise of a healthy belief in themselves as deserving, bolstered by likes and followers.

In an ironic, noxious reversal, arrogance is now rewarded, and sycophancy incentivized through the impact of AI, social media platforms, and the trickle-down effect of political leaders normalizing these behaviors. Whether fueled by self-deception, entitlement, or deliberate facade motivated by status seeking and self-promotion, the curated self manifests with a conspicuous absence of self-doubt, critical thinking, and, in this case, justifiable fear of being outed as a fraud. Now it’s the bystanders and benefactors who seem to fear exposing the fraudulence of the bona fide imposters.

The Role of Chatbots in Self-Aggrandizement

A recent study in Science found that chatbots are actually 50 percent more sycophantic than humans, though people falsely believe AI provides more objective feedback than humans. Researchers also found that more than a dozen major AI models were sycophantic, which is not surprising, since users preferred sycophantic responses over the models that didn’t agree with them (Cheng et al., 2026).

Further compounding the problem, people rated the sycophantic chatbots, in particular, as unbiased and accurate, and the chatbots that disagreed with them as negatively biased (Cheng et al., 2026).

This matters because even brief interactions with sycophantic chatbots have been found to increase people’s certainty, extreme views, and perceptions that they’re better or smarter than other people (Rathje et al., 2026).

A single interaction with a sycophantic chatbot has been found to adversely impact judgment, decision-making, and relationships—making people more likely to blame others, resist taking responsibility, and be convinced they were right (Rosenbluth, T., 2026). In relationships, people shifted from being empathic and open to considering their partner’s viewpoint to feeling entitled to accuse them of wrongdoing and refuse to apologize.

Source: Artpuppy / iStock

Psychological Motivators of the Enablers

Apart from the influence of AI, people collude in and encourage unearned confidence and inauthenticity personally, on social media, and on the political stage by supporting misleading self-promotion and egocentrism with words, likes, and follows, or implicitly through silence.

We resist exposing the truth or providing accurate feedback due to fear, cowardice, the need for self-promotion, or because it’s easier to take the path of least resistance.

A more benign contributor is a common misconception about healthy self-esteem, conflating it with narcissism, as if they were on a continuum (Brummelman & Sedikides, 2020). However, they are very distinct and cultivated through divergent socialization and parenting practices (Hyatt et al., 2028). Further, narcissism and healthy self-esteem lead to contrasting outcomes in terms of the development of psychological and emotional capacities, critical thinking, resilience, robustness, and the quality of relationships (Brummelman & Sedikides, 2020).

The Perils of Praise

Healthy self-esteem is a stable sense of self-worth. It does not involve superiority, antagonism, or status seeking, and is fostered by providing accurate feedback that emphasizes learning and self-improvement over social comparison. Narcissism, on the other hand, is nurtured by fostering overconfidence and focusing on being better than others.

Parents may unwittingly contribute to their children developing dislikable traits and narcissism by overpraising (for example, praising them no matter what they do), exaggerating how well they did, needing them to stand out, overvaluing their intelligence or specialness, rewarding the status element of their achievements, and being concerned with elevating their social status (Grapsas et al., 2020).

Source: Ignatiev / iStock

This parenting style, even if well-intended, later comes back to haunt parents, not only breeding narcissistic traits in their children such as entitlement, superiority, lying, cheating, and failure to take responsibility, but also making children vulnerable to emotional instability and symptoms such as rage, anxiety, and depression.

Further, children whose sense of self is built on a fragile foundation of illusion, requiring constant validation, admiration, and propping up, crash when faced with real-world situations like college or the job market where performance is judged on merit and results, and praise is not readily forthcoming.

In discussing the cultural rise in swagger, Sobrevilla (2026) argued that an inflated sense of power can be an adaptive reaction to feelings of existential dread and helplessness in our current world. But maintaining an illusion of grandiosity is not only off-putting but also a shallow, fragile fix that hooks people on constant admiration or status, at the inevitable cost of authentic connection, mastery, and resilience.

item.title: Nutritional Lithium Orotate for Deeper Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

Nutritional Lithium Orotate for Deeper Sleep

Good sleep is key to good health. Low-dose lithium orotate can help.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Good sleep is a must for good health.
  • Nutritional lithium orotate can aid sleep in several ways.
  • Among the many ways it affects sleep, lithium helps regulate serotonin, melatonin, and the stress response.
Source: Primipil / Stock photo ID:2268197031

A good night’s sleep isn’t just a daily period of R&R. Good sleep one of the keystones of good health, along with a diet that emphasizes whole foods, regular physical activity, and strong relationships.

People suffer many types of sleep difficulties—trouble falling asleep, trouble staying asleep, waking up early in the morning and not being able to get back to sleep, and feeling fatigued during the day from lack of deep sleep. When one or more of those difficulties are chronic—a problem suffered by an estimated 15 to 20 percent of Americans—your body and mind pay the price. Poor sleep can erode attention and memory; increase the risk of depression and anxiety; imbalance blood sugar and insulin (the hormone that regulates it), setting you up for weight gain and diabetes; damage your circulatory system, leading to heart attack and stroke; weaken immunity, making you more vulnerable to infections; and disrupt hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating nearly every bodily system. (And that’s far from a complete list!)

To add insult to injury, poor sleep can also disrupt circadian rhythms, the body’s internal 24-hour biological clocks, which some experts see as the master regulators of physical, mental, and emotional well-being. When those clocks aren’t synchronized with the daily 24-hour light-dark cycle, nearly every system in the body can get out of whack.

Source: MergeIdea / Stock photo ID:1757693235

My specialty is functional psychiatry, which focuses on biochemical individuality—treating the person rather than managing symptoms. Functional psychiatry has investigated many natural therapies that can support sleep and circadian biology. One emerging therapy is nutritional lithium orotate, a naturally occurring trace mineral. I’m not talking about lithium carbonate, the type of lithium used to treat bipolar disorder in pharmaceutical doses. I’m talking about low doses of lithium orotate, typically 1 to 2 mg a day.

How does nutritional lithium orotate help with sleep? Let me count the ways—which is a lot better than counting sheep!

How Nutritional Lithium Supports Your Sleep

Nutritional lithium can help you get a good night’s sleep in many different ways.

Supporting melatonin production. Melatonin is a hormone produced mainly by the tiny pineal gland in the brain. Its number one job is to synchronize the body’s circadian rhythms with the natural cycle of light and darkness. Melatonin production relies on the normal activity of several neurotransmitters (chemicals that help brain cells communicate), including serotonin, which itself regulates sleep, appetite, and mood. Decades of research show that lithium plays an important role in normal serotonin signaling between brain cells, thereby helping regulate melatonin.

Source: PeopleImages / Stock photo ID:1332616479

Easing the stress response. When stress isn’t overwhelming, the body produces “just the right” amounts of the stress hormone cortisol—enough to keep you alert and engaged, but not so much you feel jangled and anxious. Cortisol also follows a natural 24-hour cycle. It peaks in the morning to promote wakefulness and drops at night to allow for sleep, whereas chronic stress flattens this rhythm, leading to insomnia, nighttime awakenings, and morning exhaustion.

Research shows that lithium helps regulate HPA-axis functioning (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal); it helps balance cortisol—improving the likelihood of a good night’s sleep.

Deepening deep sleep. Deep “slow wave” sleep is powerfully restorative. During this stage, large populations of neurons fire in synchrony, producing high-amplitude, slow brain waves. Slow wave sleep is powerfully restorative: memory, immunity, waste removal, and cellular repair maximize during that time. A study in England shows that lithium increases the time you spend in slow wave sleep.

More GABA, more relaxation. Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the brain’s primary inhibitory neurotransmitter—it calms neural activity, promoting relaxation and perhaps improving sleep. Cellular and animal research shows that lithium supports GABA activity.

Balancing serotonin and dopamine. Imbalances in these two neurotransmitters have been linked to insomnia (as well as depression and anxiety). Lithium helps regulate neurotransmitter signaling, possibly reducing the nighttime worry and restlessness that can keep you up.

Cooling inflammation. A growing body of research links chronic inflammation and chronic sleep difficulty. Lithium is anti-inflammatory.

Source: Ridofranz / Stock photo ID:1029339524

Other Ways to Improve Sleep

Consider taking low-dose nutritional lithium orotate as one factor in a multifactorial approach to better sleep. Other ways to improve sleep include:

  • Consistent bedtime and wake times (for example, 11 pm and 7 am)
  • Morning sunlight exposure (to strengthen circadian rhythms)
  • Stress management (like meditation or breathwork)
  • Limiting evening exposure to blue light (primarily from screens)
  • Maximizing whole foods and minimizing ultra-processed foods
  • Adequate magnesium from whole foods like leafy greens (include a daily supplement of 250 mg of magnesium glycinate to prevent this common shortfall)

Wishing you a good night’s sleep!

item.title: The Psychology of “Maybe This Month”
item.description:
Infertility

The Psychology of “Maybe This Month”

How infertility can keep us cycling between hope, uncertainty, and grief.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Infertility creates an exhausting emotional cycle of hope, uncertainty, disappointment, and recurring grief.
  • All of the waiting during fertility treatment can intensify anxiety, uncertainty, and loss of control.
  • Infertility involves ambiguous loss: grieving the family and future you imagined while still hoping for them.

Maybe this month.

For anyone who has struggled with infertility, those three words can carry an extraordinary amount of emotional weight. Maybe there will be enough eggs. Maybe this is the month the pregnancy test will finally be positive. Maybe the embryo will be normal. Maybe it will implant. Maybe this will finally be our turn.

Infertility is unusual because it can create a chronic level of stress that involves asking you to repeatedly prepare yourself for two completely different outcomes at the same time. You’re trying to hold out hope that everything will work out while bracing yourself for the possibility of another disappointment.

And then you have to wait.

Why Waiting Is Anything but Passive

People sometimes talk about the “waiting” of infertility as though nothing is happening. But psychologically, quite a lot is happening.

Uncertainty and lack of control are recurring themes in research on the psychological experience of infertility and fertility treatment. Women describe not knowing whether treatment will work, struggling to control the uncontrollable, and trying to maintain hope despite unsuccessful treatment (Aiello et al., 2025).

During the days between treatment and results, the brain can go into overdrive.

You may jump every time the phone rings, hoping or worrying that it’s the doctor calling. You check and recheck your phone to make sure you didn't somehow miss a call from the clinic. You may monitor every physical sensation, then search every website for answers that only leave you more overwhelmed. You may take a home pregnancy test much earlier than your blood test scheduled at the clinic.

And you dare to let your mind fantasize about the future. If this worked, when would I be due? When could we tell our families? Would the baby arrive before or after my best friend’s wedding? Will we finally be able to celebrate the holidays with joy?

And just as quickly, you tell yourself not to jinx anything with thoughts of excitement or hope. What if it didn't work? Can I do this again? How many more chances do we have? What if I never become a parent?

This is one of the cruel paradoxes of waiting during infertility: Nothing has happened yet, but emotionally, you’ve lived through multiple possible futures.

The Emotional Whiplash of Infertility

Then the result arrives. Sometimes it’s wonderful news. But sometimes you face another disappointment: a canceled cycle, an embryo that stops developing, an abnormal genetic result, a negative pregnancy test, or another piece of information that changes the path forward.

Then there is grief.

Infertility has long been conceptualized as a form of ambiguous loss. People may be grieving an anticipated child, an imagined family, a reproductive identity, or a future they expected would already be a reality, while the possibility of achieving that future still remains (Burns, 1987).

And infertility often doesn't give people much time to grieve because they don’t have the luxury of time. Soon another cycle begins. And suddenly there is possibility again.

Hope. Waiting. Uncertainty. Disappointment. Grief. Hope Again.

Recent qualitative research describes this tension particularly well: Women undergoing fertility treatment report struggling with uncertainty and lack of control while simultaneously trying to maintain hope and persist with treatment despite repeated failures (Aiello et al., 2025).

Over months or years, repeatedly moving through this cycle can become psychologically exhausting. Many losses in life have a clearer dividing line between before and after, with months or years to reconcile these changes. Infertility often does not.

You may be grieving what hasn't happened while simultaneously trying to believe that it still might.

“I'm Not Getting My Hopes Up This Time”

After enough disappointment, patients often tell me some version of “I'm not going to get my hopes up this time.” It makes perfect sense; if hope precedes pain, perhaps hoping less will make the pain hurt less. Unfortunately, emotions rarely cooperate with bargains like these.

You can insist that this cycle is “just another cycle” and still feel completely out of control during the two-week wait. You can prepare yourself for bad news and still be devastated when it arrives.

Hope isn't a mistake, and disappointment doesn't mean you’re being punished for hoping too much.

Learning to Hold Hope and Uncertainty Together

The psychological task may be learning to hold hope and uncertainty at the same time.

Try making room for both:

I really hope this works.

I don't know yet whether it will.

And I don't have to figure out today what I will do if it doesn't.

That last sentence can be particularly important.

An anxious brain often tries to protect us by solving future problems before they exist. But mentally living through every possible bad outcome doesn't necessarily make us better prepared for it. Sometimes it simply means experiencing the emotional consequences of an outcome that hasn't happened, which takes up the space where hope could exist.

When you notice your thoughts moving months or years into an imagined future, gently bring the time horizon closer. What do I actually know today? What decision actually needs to be made today? What do I need to get through today?

You Are Not Starting Over

When another cycle begins, people often talk about “starting again.” But psychologically, you aren't starting from the beginning; you’re carrying everything that came before:

The previous negative tests.

The losses.

The procedures.

The bills.

The hope you tried not to feel.

The disappointment you thought you were prepared for.

And the remarkable fact that some part of you may still be capable of saying “Maybe this month.”

Research consistently shows that infertility and its treatment can involve uncertainty, anxiety, grief, loss of control, isolation, and disruption to one's expected life course (Burns, 1987; Aiello et al., 2025). The answer isn't to stop caring or to stop hoping but to find a way to leave some room for the life you’re living now while you wait to discover what comes next.
