item.title: Can We Overcome the Doom of Optimization?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can We Overcome the Doom of Optimization?

Four steps to preserve the delight of imperfection

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • AI optimization leads to average, bland outputs, erasing uniqueness and delight.
  • Yet people instinctively prefer imperfect, human-made works over flawless AI outputs.
  • Preserve imperfection: create before using AI, and consciously keep quirks and flaws.
AI-optimized output drifts toward the same middle, the highest common denominator. The essence goes missing along the way.
Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT. 2026

Slice open a supermarket tomato. Red to the edges, geometrically obedient, flavored like the faint rumor of tomato. Breeders nowadays “built” it for the truck, the shelf, the long wait under fluorescent light; they are optimized to offend nobody. Keep that tomato image at the back of your mind as you read on—the words, pictures, songs, and videos crossing our screens are ripening with the same logic.

The Likeliest Everything

Optimization has one favorite move: pick the likeliest next thing. The likeliest word, the likeliest pixel, the likeliest chord. Likeliest means most common, and most common means average. Every polished output drifts toward the same middle, the highest common denominator, with every corner sanded and every seam hidden. Each piece arrives wearing a fresh outfit over the same skeleton.

Researchers have begun to measure that polishing process. In a Science Advances study, writers were asked to compose short stories with and without generative AI. Writers with the most access to AI tools produced stories scoring higher for novelty and usefulness—their deliverables also resembled one another. While the individual stories improved on average, the shelf as a whole deteriorated as it grew monotonous. It’s a modern version of a classic social dilemma: each writer has good reason to use the tool and benefits in the short run; the sum of those choices is to the detriment of everyone as the outcome narrows what the rest of us get to read.

Music arrived at the destination of blandness first. Analyzing popular recordings from 1955 to 2010, researchers found the sound palette homogenizing, pitch transitions narrowing, and loudness climbing. Producers chasing the same radio-ready sound managed it with nothing fancier than human imitation. AI-powered software now does the imitating at industrial speed.

Recent research found that blandness increases over time as newer models are trained on the output of earlier models. What is rare and quirky—the dialect, the odd joke, the sentence that takes a wrong turn or finds an unexpected twist—is washed out. Over time, a system that feeds on its own average gradually starves itself for the variety it cannot produce.

What Fast Food Taught the Tongue

Food has followed the missing sound of the music, walking down the lane of optimization long before ChatGPT and co. came along. In 2019, Kevin Hall’s team at the NIH housed 20 adults for a month and fed them ultra-processed meals for two weeks and unprocessed meals for two weeks. The menus matched for calories, sugar, fat, fiber, and macronutrients.

On the ultra-processed menu, volunteers ate roughly 500 extra calories a day, ate faster, and gained about two pounds. Same label, different appetite. Palates adapt to whatever surrounds them. A generation weaned on engineered salt, fat, and sweetness meets a ripe fig, a bitter green, or a funky cheese as a stranger at the door. Fast food tuned millions of tongues for sweet, salty, and easy-to-chew food.

Our eyes and minds are being tuned the same way. Think of the email that opens with a wish for your well-being and closes with an offer to connect. The LinkedIn post that breaks every sentence onto its own line for drama. The product photo where every face glows like a ring light. The voiceover with that one upbeat cadence, borrowed by ten thousand explainers. Each item is fine. Taken together, they form a mental diet, and the cognitive palate that consumes it begins to expect it. But our subconscious is duped less easily.

Hunger follows monotony, always. Slow food began as a response to a burger stand near Rome’s Spanish Steps. Sourdough starters now bubble on kitchen counters, vinyl has a second life, and a lopsided loaf counts as a selling point.

The same appetite shows up in the lab. In various experiments, participants judged paintings that were all AI-made, and others labeled as human-created; the latter won higher marks, with the widest margins on meaning and worth. The sad aspect of this is that the label alone was enough to trigger the verdict. Humans crave evidence of a hand, a history, a life behind the work. Yet they are keen to gobble down the average that suits their expectations. (Recent research on emotional support found a similar logic; participants indicated their preference for psychological advice by humans, judging the AI bots as more emphatic.)

Imperfection carries information. The voice that cracks on the high note tells you a “someone” is singing. A sentence that lurches and recovers shows a mind at work. The wobble in a hand-thrown mug may record the afternoon vibe it was made with. Accent, hesitation, a joke that lands a beat late, a photograph with a thumb in the corner—these are flavors, and a flavor needs a particular organically evolving place to come from. A thing made everywhere in general comes from nowhere in particular.

Keep the Real of You Alive

Here is a simple practical way to keep that place in you alive:

  1. Write first drafts, record first takes, and sketch first ideas before consulting a machine. Unmediated, your thoughts have the highest chance to still carry your fingerprints (although our ongoing exposure to social media, AI slop, and other mediatic optimized channels is inevitably leaving a trace in our language and perception, unless we are acutely vigilant).
  2. If you want a tool to tidy the edges, bring it in on the second pass.
  3. Consciously reject any edit that sands off a quirk you liked! Leave one flaw standing on purpose, whether a digression, a regional word, an unretouched photo, or a voice memo with a kettle whistling behind it. Once a week, share something unfinished with a living person and watch which rough edges they remember. As AI is increasingly becoming all-pervasive, you may want to keep a file of your own phrases: the words your grandmother used, the metaphor you reach for when tired, the joke only your friends get.

Hybrid flourishing needs humans to experience and nurture it. That human seat belongs to a single, specific, uneven someone. Each of us is an ambassador for the uniqueness of us. Let’s keep that special spark alive.

item.title: Living With a Needy Partner
item.description:
Relationships

Living With a Needy Partner

How to to preserve your sense of self with a clingy loved one.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • Needy individuals often make their partners feel burdened and used.
  • Their partners often develop feelings of resentment and or burnout.
  • This challenges the relationship and may end it.
  • Compassionate rebalancing of asymmetrical relationships can make them more gratifying and more stable.

Healthy individuals covet their independence. They place minimal burden on their partners because they prefer to do things for themselves. Other individuals prefer to have their partners serve and take care of them. Dependent individuals often place a persistent burden on their partners, who eventually either develop resentment or burn out. This process compromises relationship quality and threatens its survival. If your partner is very needy and you feel resentment or burnout, you can act now to avoid disintegrating the relationship. Appropriate, consistent, and compassionate boundaries will improve relationship quality and increase durability.

People can find themselves in asymmetrical relationships. This occurs when one partner gives while the other takes—disproportionately. This asymmetry violates a core concept of partnership: equality.

Rebalance asymmetrical relationships before you burn out.
Source: Image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay

Partners of persistently needy people tend to develop resentment, or feel exploited and taken advantage of. They often feel their efforts are not spontaneously returned, so they ask for whatever they get. They get angry when they ask and are refused.

Burnout occurs when the overburdened partner surrenders to the needy person's demands. They do so to avoid dramatic expressions of need and disappointment when those needs aren't met. They surrender to the demands and do whatever they are asked or told without thinking about it. This is where loss of self increases.

Without resistance, the needy person tends to add more and more needs to the partner’s burden. These needs often include emotional ones such as constant attention or persistent validation—beyond the pragmatic needs of daily living. Eventually, the burdened spouse’s life becomes in the service of the partner. Dissociation and depression often increase as they reach the breaking point. The point where the relationship is no longer tolerable. At this point, they either get out or get sick. Both eventually interrupt the process and threaten relationship survival.

If you have a needy partner and you feel that you are headed to your breaking point, you might try the following:

Step One: Self-Reflect

Examine your own reasons for allowing the type of relationship to occur. Ask yourself the following questions:

  • Do I seek validation by pleasing or serving others?
  • Is serving others and making self-sacrifice my primary way of expressing love?
  • Am I more afraid of hurting others than being hurt myself?
  • Am I afraid that if I don’t satisfy my partner in every way, I will not be loved?

If you answer any of these questions affirmatively, you may be a people-pleaser. If so, stopping this behavior will help your partner. This may require your own personal therapy to understand this aspect of your behavior, but you are going to have to learn to say no to sustain the relationship and get relief.

Step Two: Set Appropriate Boundaries

If your partner is comfortable with the asymmetry in the relationship, then you will have to be the agent of change. Decide what you need to continue the relationship; get what you need, and give at your comfort level. Express this to your partner in clear and compassionate terms. Make this clear: You need certain things to sustain the relationship.

Rebalancing both what you give and what you take will produce the best result. Reduce your burden; stop doing what your partner can do for themselves. For example, if you and your partner are watching television and your partner asks you to get them a glass of water, you can say, “I will next time I get up.” This reduces the burden to close to zero. If your partner routinely leaves dirty clothing on the floor for you to pick up, ask them to put it in the hamper rather than doing it yourself.

Next, increase what you take from the relationship. For example, you may find that your partner’s demands interfere with your physical wellness. You don’t have time to exercise regularly or make preventive doctor and dentist visits. Eventually, you will get sick if this persists. You work to prioritize your medical appointments and exercise three times per week. You don’t need to ask permission; schedule it. When your partner requests or demands your time during these periods, you are not available during those times. This boundary applies to patterns of behaviors more than specific events. You can make your partner breakfast in bed on their birthday, but don’t do it every day.

Step Three: Communicate With Your Partner

Your efforts to balance your relationship will be noticed. Be prepared to explain to your partner that it is better for you, better for them, and crucial for the relationship that it be better balanced. For your partner, it is empowering, and it encourages autonomy, which promotes mental health. You will be a happier partner and able to give your love more freely. The relationship will benefit from greater stability, better balance, and cooperative negotiation.

item.title: AI Didn't Write This Post
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Didn't Write This Post

Artificial intelligence poses ethical problems for students and faculty.

Posted October 7, 2026

Key points
  • AI makes plagiarism easy.
  • AI is often used by faculty and administrators to enhance their own writing.
  • What constitutes plagiarism isn't a new concern; it needs to be considered again in the age of AI.
  • What is needed is a thoughtful examination, not condemnation.

This article wasn’t written by AI but by me, the person whose name appears at the top of the page. You have my word for it.

But let’s say that what you are reading really is a product of AI. Would it make any difference if all the facts were correct, no grammatical or spelling errors, clear writing and the presentation coherent and cogent? If you were interested in the subject, I suspect not. Whether written by a person or AI would likely be irrelevant.

For teachers and others concerned with not only the moral implications of cheating but also the cognitive side of development, who wrote an assigned paper is a big deal. For real learning to occur, it isn’t only the end products that matter but also the method by which they are created. Education is more than learning how to be a copyist or stenographer. Do the students understand what they have submitted? Have they learned to think for themselves? In this way, turning in a paper lifted from the internet or copied straight from another source is no different than run-of-the-mill plagiarism. It is a form of cheating, claiming something that isn’t yours. Deception undermines trust, a necessity for functioning.

A good education teaches students how to recognize relevant information, arrange ideas coherently, make logical arguments, and reach reasonable conclusions. While critical thinking can develop under various pedagogical methods, as explained by Williams College professor Joe Cruz, when AI does the writing (and thinking) for students, they are at risk of diminishing creative and critical thinking skills, according to other researchers.

Students at Dartmouth College have turned the tables on professors and administrators, calling for their provost to be investigated over his use of AI for several articles he had written. In his defense, Dr. Snell, Dartmouth’s provost, admitted to using AI but has said that he used it only to refine his work.

The contretemps over Provost Snell and others highlights the ambiguity surrounding the uses of AI. If Dr. Snell is telling the truth that he only used AI to enhance articles in his publications, is this different from students who use it to improve the quality of their writing? How much editing crosses a line into plagiarism? If a writer narrows down research options by using Google Scholar, is this an ethical breach?

Years before AI entered the fray, plagiarism was a fraught subject. In 2002, for example, Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Doris Kearns Goodwin’s best-seller about the Kennedys used many passages verbatim from another writer’s work. Her defense? She took notes by hand and couldn’t distinguish between her paraphrasing and quoting without attribution. She defended herself by saying that citation mistakes can happen. Kearns reputation suffered a setback but only temporarily. Soon after, her near-celebrity status resumed untarnished.

How should AI be regulated in education? One thing is clear: publishing an article as if you wrote it when you didn’t is cheating. One hopes that the controversy swirling around Dr. Snell and others ends, not with condemnation, but with clarifying, as best one can, what is acceptable and what is not. Times call for thoughtful discourse, not censure. If college professors aren’t sure about the rules, how can you blame students?
